channel.title: Model Compression
channel.description: Technical notes by Jaehun Ryu, a deep learning compiler engineer, on LLM inference, KV caches, compilers, C++, AI papers, and open-source code.

item.title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
item.description:
Paper

AutoCompress: Model Compression That Puts Serving Constraints Directly into the Search Objective

Introduction

When engineers deploy a large language model to a real service, the first question they hit is not “how much should we shrink it?” but “which axis should we shrink, and by how much, to survive on this device and this workload?” AutoCompress (NVIDIA, arXiv:2611.08290) turns that question into a cost model measured directly in the serving engine, and finds the answer by putting latency, throughput, and memory limits into the architecture search objective. This post starts from the problem that “parameter count alone cannot predict serving cost,” then covers examples of what remains and what disappears when one axis is narrowed, each step of the method, and results from three deployment scenarios and the 120B single-GPU case, in that order.

item.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

Speculative decoding is a technique that commits multiple tokens together when a large model is invoked once, accelerating language model decoding where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. This paper points out that public implementations of this technique fail to capture much of the permissible speedup, and has a coding agent re-measure the bottleneck for each deployment environment and discover optimizations on its own. The result is a large increase in speedup for both single requests and batching, without training or loss of output quality.

item.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
item.description: Paper Recent language models keep increasing the amount of information packed into a single vocabulary entry. Per-layer embeddings (PLE), first introduced in Gemma 3n, carried over to Gemma 4: instead of a single input-layer vector per vocabulary item, each decoder layer has a different learned vector. This post examines OPTIC, which shrinks this table by about 100× while retaining most of the original performance, starting from the problem setting and proceeding through a small example, the method, results, and limitations.

item.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

Observing that LLM autoregressive decoding is memory-bound, this work collects the calibration for pruning not from “fixed text” but from “tokens the model generates itself,” and attaches a decoding-specific (SpMV) $N{:}M$ kernel to it, achieving up to $1.48\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup.

item.title: CoVeR: Coverage-Based Token Pruning for Multi-View 3D Reasoning in VLMs
item.description:
Paper

CoVeR: Coverage-Based Pruning That Cuts Visual Tokens of Multi-View 3D Reasoning by up to 92% Using Geometry Alone

One-Line Summary (TL;DR)

Rendering a 3D scene into multi-view images and feeding them to a 2D VLM makes tokens explode proportionally to the number of views. CoVeR selects tokens that cover the entire scene uniformly using only the tokens’ 3D coordinates, with no training, retaining 93.5% of the original performance with only about 8% of the tokens, and outperforming the existing SOTA by an average of 3.9%p (source: Abstract, §4.1).

item.title: SQS: Bayesian DNN Compression through Sparse Quantized Sub-distributions
item.description:
Paper

SQS: Fusing Pruning and Quantization into One Bayesian Learning — Where Spike-and-Slab Meets GMM

TL;DR — Doing pruning and low-bit quantization separately leaves redundancy on the table. SQS couples a spike-and-slab prior with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) into a single variational learning scheme, achieving higher compression at the same bit-width and lower accuracy loss at the same compression ratio.

item.title: X-AuT: Progressive Audio-Encoder Compression for Speech LLMs with Cross-Scale Distillation
item.description:
Paper

X-AuT: Pruning Audio Encoders in Speech LLMs with Behavioral Probes and Cross-Scale Distillation

TL;DR

X-AuT is a framework that progressively prunes the audio encoder (audio Transformer) of a speech LLM from 18 → 16 → 14 layers, selecting recoverable layer combinations with short behavioral probes, and recovering the loss via cross-scale distillation (1.7B teacher → 0.6B student) followed by 3-stage recovery. The 14-layer model cuts audio-tower parameters by 20.7% while keeping the macro error rate nearly intact at 5.75% (baseline 5.61%); the 16-layer model actually beats the baseline at 5.27% (source: Abstract, §1).
